questions.stem: Which sequence lists the levels of organisation in the human body from least to most complex?
options: Cell, organ, tissue, system, organism
Organelle, organ, tissue, cell, system
Cell, tissue, organ, system, organism
Tissue, cell, organ, organism, system
questions.explanation: Similar cells form a tissue, several tissues form an organ, organs work together as a system, and the systems together make up the organism. Placing organs before tissues reverses two levels.

questions.stem: The small intestine contains epithelial lining, smooth muscle, connective tissue and nerves. Which term best describes the small intestine?
options: A cell group, because each layer carries out absorption
An organ, because it is made of several tissues working together
A tissue, because its cells all share one digestive function
A system, because it contains more than one type of cell
questions.explanation: An organ is a structure made of two or more tissue types that together carry out a function. The small intestine is one organ within the digestive system, not a system on its own.

questions.stem: During exercise the respiratory and circulatory systems both increase their activity. What does this show about body systems?
options: Only one system can increase its activity at a time during physical effort
Systems interact so that cells get the inputs and lose the outputs of metabolism
Each system works independently and responds only to its own local signals
The respiratory system can replace the circulatory system when demand is high
questions.explanation: Muscle cells need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide during exercise, so breathing and heart rate both rise. Body systems are linked, and together they maintain the conditions cells need.

questions.stem: In which organelle does most of the ATP from aerobic respiration form?
options: Lysosome
Mitochondrion
Ribosome
Golgi body
questions.explanation: The later stages of aerobic respiration happen in the mitochondria, which produce most of the cell's ATP. Ribosomes make proteins, not ATP.

questions.stem: What is the function of ribosomes?
options: Storing the cell's genetic information
Joining amino acids to make proteins
Packaging proteins into vesicles for export
Breaking down worn-out organelles
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis, where amino acids are joined into polypeptides. Packaging and export is the job of the Golgi body.

questions.stem: Cells in the pancreas secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes. Which pair of organelles would be especially abundant in these cells?
options: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum and lysosomes
Centrioles and the nucleolus
Lysosomes and the cell membrane only
Rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins: they are made on ribosomes attached to rough endoplasmic reticulum, then modified and packaged for secretion by the Golgi body. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum mainly makes lipids.

questions.stem: What is the main role of lysosomes in a human cell?
options: Digesting worn-out organelles and engulfed material
Making lipids and steroid hormones for use in the cell
Producing ATP when the cell is short of oxygen
Controlling which genes are switched on in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs of digestive enzymes that break down old organelles and material taken in by endocytosis. Lipid and steroid synthesis happens on smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.stem: Which organelle contains the DNA that directs most of the cell's activities and is surrounded by a double membrane with pores?
options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
Vacuole
Nucleus
Golgi body
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds most of the cell's DNA and is bounded by a nuclear envelope with pores that let mRNA leave. Mitochondria also have a double membrane but no pores of this kind.

questions.stem: A cell is given a poison that stops its mitochondria working. Which process would be most directly affected?
options: Osmosis of water into the cell
Facilitated diffusion of glucose into the cell
Active transport of ions into the cell
Simple diffusion of oxygen into the cell
questions.explanation: Active transport needs ATP, and without working mitochondria the cell's ATP supply falls sharply. Diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis are passive and need no ATP.

questions.stem: Which list gives inputs a human cell must take in and outputs it must remove to keep metabolising efficiently?
options: In: oxygen and glucose. Out: carbon dioxide and water
In: carbon dioxide and water. Out: oxygen and glucose
In: oxygen and carbon dioxide. Out: glucose and water
In: glucose and carbon dioxide. Out: oxygen and water
questions.explanation: Cells need oxygen and nutrients such as glucose for respiration, and must remove its waste products, carbon dioxide and water. Taking in carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen describes photosynthesis, which human cells do not carry out.

questions.stem: In the fluid mosaic model, what forms the basic structure of the cell membrane?
options: A single layer of protein
A layer of cellulose
A double layer of cholesterol
A phospholipid bilayer
questions.explanation: The membrane is a double layer of phospholipids with proteins scattered through it like tiles in a mosaic. Cellulose forms plant cell walls, not membranes.

questions.stem: In the fluid mosaic model, what does the word fluid refer to?
options: Its phospholipids and many proteins can move sideways within the layer
It is made mainly of water held between two layers of protein
Its pores open and close to let fluid flow freely through it
It dissolves and reforms each time a material crosses it
questions.explanation: The phospholipids and many of the proteins are not fixed in place and drift laterally, so the membrane behaves like a fluid. Its hydrophobic core actually keeps water from crossing freely.

questions.stem: How are the phospholipids arranged in the cell membrane?
options: Hydrophilic heads face the watery fluid on each side; hydrophobic tails face inwards
Hydrophobic tails face the watery fluid on each side; hydrophilic heads face inwards
Heads and tails alternate along a single layer that faces the cytoplasm
All heads face the outside of the cell and all tails face the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Phosphate heads are attracted to water, so they face the tissue fluid and the cytosol, while the fatty acid tails avoid water and form the membrane's core. That core is why charged and polar substances cross poorly.

questions.stem: What is the role of glycoproteins on the outer surface of the cell membrane?
options: Holding the phospholipid tails together in the bilayer
Producing ATP for active transport across the membrane
Acting as markers that let cells recognise each other
Forming channels for water to move through by osmosis
questions.explanation: Glycoproteins carry carbohydrate chains that act as identity markers and receptors, for example in blood group antigens and immune recognition. Water channels are formed by other proteins called aquaporins.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines osmosis?
options: The net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration
The net movement of solute across a partially permeable membrane from higher to lower solute concentration
The movement of water against its gradient using energy from ATP across a membrane
The movement of any substance from a region of high to low concentration without a membrane
questions.explanation: Osmosis is specifically the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane, towards the side with more dissolved solute. Movement of solutes down a gradient is diffusion, not osmosis.

questions.stem: Which substance crosses the cell membrane mainly by simple diffusion through the phospholipid bilayer?
options: Oxygen
Glucose
Sodium ions
Proteins
questions.explanation: Small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in the lipid bilayer and diffuse straight through. Glucose and ions need carrier or channel proteins.

questions.stem: Glucose enters red blood cells down its concentration gradient through specific carrier proteins, without using ATP. What is this process?
options: Endocytosis
Facilitated diffusion
Active transport
Simple diffusion
questions.explanation: Movement down a gradient through a protein, with no ATP, is facilitated diffusion. Active transport also uses carrier proteins but moves substances against their gradient using ATP.

questions.stem: Cells lining the small intestine take in glucose even when its concentration is higher inside the cell than in the gut. Which process allows this?
options: Osmosis, driven by the water potential gradient
Simple diffusion through the phospholipid bilayer
Active transport, using ATP and carrier proteins
Facilitated diffusion, using channel proteins
questions.explanation: Moving glucose from low to high concentration is against its gradient, which needs energy from ATP and a carrier protein. Diffusion of any kind can only move a substance down its gradient.

questions.stem: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium by surrounding it with its membrane. What is this process called?
options: Exocytosis, a type of vesicular transport
Facilitated diffusion through a carrier
Pinocytosis, the uptake of liquid droplets
Phagocytosis, a type of endocytosis
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis ('cell eating') is endocytosis of large solid particles. Pinocytosis is also endocytosis but takes in droplets of fluid, and exocytosis moves material out of the cell.

questions.stem: Nerve cells release neurotransmitter molecules stored in vesicles when the vesicles fuse with the cell membrane. What is this process?
options: Exocytosis
Endocytosis
Phagocytosis
Facilitated diffusion
questions.explanation: Exocytosis releases the contents of a vesicle to the outside when its membrane fuses with the cell membrane. Endocytosis is the reverse, bringing material into the cell in a vesicle.

questions.stem: Red blood cells are placed in a salt solution far more concentrated than blood plasma. What happens to them, and why?
options: They shrink and crenate, because water leaves them by osmosis
They swell and burst, because water enters them by osmosis
They shrink, because salt moves out of them by active transport
They stay the same, because their membranes are impermeable to salt
questions.explanation: The solution has a higher solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis and they shrivel. Bursting happens in pure water, where water moves in.

questions.stem: A patient needs fluid through a drip. Why is the drip solution made isotonic with blood plasma?
options: So that salt diffuses out of the blood cells and lowers their concentration
So the blood cells swell slightly and carry more oxygen to the tissues
So there is no net osmosis into or out of blood cells, which keeps them intact
So that water is actively pumped into the blood cells to rehydrate them
questions.explanation: When the solute concentration outside equals that inside the cells there is no net water movement, so cells neither swell and burst nor shrink. Pure water would cause red cells to take in water and haemolyse.

questions.stem: Which comparison of facilitated diffusion and active transport is correct?
options: Both move substances against a gradient, but only one uses ATP
Both use membrane proteins, but only active transport needs ATP
Both need ATP, but only active transport uses membrane proteins
Neither uses proteins, but active transport moves larger molecules
questions.explanation: Both processes rely on specific membrane proteins. Facilitated diffusion is passive and moves substances down their gradient, while active transport uses ATP to move them against it.

questions.stem: A cube-shaped model cell has sides of 3 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 x 3 x 3 = 54 cm² and volume = 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 cm³, so the ratio is 54 : 27 = 2 : 1. Writing 1 : 2 inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: Why are most human cells very small?
options: A small cell has a low surface area to volume ratio, so it loses less heat and water
Small cells need no transport proteins because materials cross freely
Small cells carry out no metabolism, so they need very few materials
A small cell has a high surface area to volume ratio, so exchange can meet its needs
questions.explanation: As a cell grows its volume rises faster than its surface area, so a large cell could not exchange materials fast enough for its metabolism. A small size keeps the ratio high.

questions.stem: Agar cubes of side 1 cm and 3 cm contain an indicator that changes colour as an acid diffuses in. After 4 minutes the 1 cm cube is fully coloured but the 3 cm cube has a clear core. What is the best explanation?
options: The larger cube has less surface per unit volume, so acid takes longer to reach its centre
Acid diffuses more slowly into a larger cube because its surface is less permeable
The larger cube has a smaller total surface area, so less acid can enter it
The indicator reacts more slowly in the larger cube because it is much more dilute there
questions.explanation: Acid enters at the same rate per unit of surface, but the 3 cm cube has a lower surface area to volume ratio and a greater distance to its centre. Its total surface area is actually larger, not smaller.

questions.stem: Oxygen diffuses from the blood into a respiring muscle cell. What keeps the rate of diffusion high?
options: The blood carries oxygen slowly, which keeps the outside concentration low
The cell uses oxygen in respiration, which keeps a steep concentration gradient
The cell stores oxygen in vesicles, which keeps the inside concentration high
The cell pumps oxygen in with ATP, which raises the inside concentration
questions.explanation: Diffusion is faster when the concentration difference is large. Because the cell keeps using oxygen, its internal concentration stays low and the gradient from blood to cell stays steep.

questions.stem: Which property of a substance makes it cross the phospholipid bilayer most easily?
options: Being small and lipid soluble
Being large and water soluble
Carrying a strong electric charge
Being a large protein molecule
questions.explanation: The hydrophobic core lets small, lipid-soluble molecules such as oxygen and steroid hormones pass, but blocks ions and large polar molecules. Charged particles need channel or carrier proteins.

questions.stem: In an investigation, the rate of diffusion of a dye into gelatine blocks is measured at 10 °C and 30 °C. The rate is higher at 30 °C. Which explanation fits?
options: Particles have more kinetic energy at higher temperature, so they spread faster
The concentration gradient becomes steeper as the temperature rises
Warmer gelatine has a higher surface area to volume ratio than cool gelatine
The dye is actively transported into the blocks at higher temperatures
questions.explanation: Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of particles, so they move and spread faster. Gelatine has no living cells, so active transport cannot be involved.

questions.stem: Each villus of the small intestine is covered in cells with microvilli. How does this structure affect absorption?
options: It reduces the concentration gradient so absorption is controlled
It greatly increases the surface area available for exchange
It greatly reduces the distance between the gut and the liver
It slows the passage of food so that enzymes can act for longer
questions.explanation: Folds, villi and microvilli multiply the area of membrane in contact with digested food, so far more nutrient can be absorbed per second. They do not change the distance to the liver.

questions.stem: Which list gives the four basic tissue types of the human body?
options: Epithelial, skeletal, muscular and blood
Connective, cardiac, lymphatic and nervous
Glandular, connective, muscular and skin
Epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous
questions.explanation: All body tissues are grouped into four basic types: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous. Blood, bone and cartilage are all kinds of connective tissue.

questions.stem: Which tissue type covers body surfaces and lines body cavities, tubes and organs?
options: Connective tissue
Nervous tissue
Muscular tissue
Epithelial tissue
questions.explanation: Epithelial tissue forms coverings and linings, such as the skin's outer layer and the lining of the gut and airways. Connective tissue supports and binds other tissues.

questions.stem: Blood, bone, cartilage and adipose tissue look very different. Why are they all classed as connective tissue?
options: Their cells are spread through a matrix that they produce
They all contract to move parts of the body when stimulated
They all transmit electrical impulses from one place to another
Their cells are packed tightly together in sheets with no matrix
questions.explanation: Connective tissues consist of cells scattered in a matrix: liquid plasma in blood, mineralised matrix in bone, and a firm gel in cartilage. Tightly packed sheets of cells describe epithelium.

questions.stem: The walls of the alveoli are made of a single layer of very thin, flat cells. Which tissue is this, and why does it suit the alveoli?
options: Ciliated columnar epithelium, sweeping mucus out of the lungs
Dense connective tissue, giving strength to resist stretching
Simple squamous epithelium, giving a short diffusion distance
Stratified squamous epithelium, giving protection from abrasion
questions.explanation: One layer of flat cells gives gases the shortest possible path between air and blood. Stratified squamous epithelium has many layers and suits surfaces that are rubbed, such as the skin.

questions.stem: Which type of muscle tissue is striated, under voluntary control and attached to bones?
options: Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Visceral muscle
Skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary. Cardiac muscle is also striated but involuntary, and smooth (visceral) muscle in organ walls is unstriated and involuntary.

questions.stem: Nervous tissue is made of neurons and supporting cells. What is the main function of neurons?
options: Transmitting electrical impulses that carry information
Contracting to move the skeleton and maintain posture
Secreting mucus and enzymes onto internal surfaces
Storing fat and insulating the body against heat loss
questions.explanation: Neurons are specialised to conduct electrical impulses rapidly, linking receptors, the central nervous system and effectors. Storing fat is the role of adipose connective tissue.

questions.stem: A tissue sample contains long, branching, striated cells joined end to end by intercalated discs. Where in the body did it most likely come from?
options: The wall of the stomach
A muscle of the thigh
The lining of the trachea
The wall of the heart
questions.explanation: Branching striated cells linked by intercalated discs are the signature of cardiac muscle, found only in the heart. Thigh muscles are skeletal, with long unbranched multinucleate fibres.
